title: Solecism of number in Hosea: plural tears, singular address
english: Scripture sometimes speaks with solecisms of wording that unsettle a reader and tempt the guess that the text was not written rightly or consistently. Some even dare, under the pretext of correction, to alter sayings and shift the sense that already lies in wording that looks consistent.

Here a similar case has fallen on the wording before us, so we must see the sense that lies in it. Hosea first speaks in the plural: "[[They wept and begged me >> Bible:Hosea 5:15]]" (sense of the plural tears), and again in the plural: "While I was in the house, they found me." Then he continues in the singular: "And there it was spoken toward him."

A reader fixed on bare wording and suspecting a slip would either pluralize the last clause or singularize what came before—reading on as if it said "spoken toward them," that is, toward those who wept…

title: Genesis singular permission, plural prohibition
english: …and those who begged, and who, while he was in the house, found God. From like sayings we can show that this too is said consistently.

In Genesis, when God commands Adam, he says: "[[From every tree of the garden you may freely eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat; for in the day you eat of it you shall surely die >> Bible:Genesis 2:16-17]]."

There too he begins in the singular—"you may freely eat"—and then shifts to the plural prohibition and warning. When the command is about the life-keeping precept, he addresses Adam in the singular. Those who walk according to God and hold his commandments, even if many, by…

title: Many become one when they find God
english: …being of one mind, the many are one. That is why a command about the good is spoken in the singular—"you may freely eat"—but when the text turns to transgression it shifts to the plural: "You shall not eat; in the day you eat, you shall die."

So here also: while they still weep and beg toward God, the wording stays plural—"They wept and begged"—but when they find God it no longer says "spoken toward them," but "toward him." For the many have already become one in finding God and hearing his word.

The single person, when he sins, is multiplied—split from God, divided, fallen from unity—whereas the many who follow God's commandments are one. So the Apostle testifies: "[[We who are many are one bread, one >> Bible:1 Corinthians 10:17]]…"

title: One body, one faith; tower of many stones
english: …body; and again: "[[one God, one Christ, one faith, one baptism >> Bible:Ephesians 4:5-6]]"; and elsewhere: "[[all are one in Christ Jesus >> Bible:Galatians 3:28]]"; and again: "[[I betrothed you to one husband, to present a pure virgin to the Lord >> Bible:2 Corinthians 11:2]]."

That those who please the Lord are one is clear from the Savior's prayer for his disciples: "[[Holy Father, grant that as you and I are one, they also may be one in us >> Bible:John 17:11]]." When the holy are called members of one another, what are they if not one body?
In the Shepherd too the tower is built of many stones yet appears as one stone: Scripture signifies the concord and unity that come from many.
